svg.title: Pathogens & disease
svg.desc: Four pathogen groups: Bacteria: cells multiply and may release toxins. Viruses: reproduce inside living cells, damaging them. Fungi and protists can cause disease too. Communicable diseases pass between organisms. Break the transmission route: Contact → hygiene/isolation. Contaminated water/food → sanitation, clean preparation and cooking. Airborne droplets → reduce exposure/isolate infected people. Vectors → prevent bites and breeding. Vaccination reduces susceptible hosts; match prevention to the pathogen’s route. Measles: Virus spread by inhaling droplets from coughs/sneezes. Fever and red rash; complications can be fatal. Vaccination in childhood reduces illness and spread. HIV → immune damage: Spread by sexual contact or exchanged body fluids, including shared needles. Initially flu-like illness. Attacks immune cells; AIDS is severe late-stage damage, with vulnerability to infections/cancers. Antiretroviral drugs control multiplication. Condoms and avoiding needle sharing reduce spread. Bacterial infections: Salmonella: contaminated food; bacteria/toxins cause fever, cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea. Hygiene/cooking and poultry vaccination help. Gonorrhoea: sexual contact; yellow/green discharge and painful urination. Condoms and suitable antibiotics help; resistant strains limit treatment. Malaria: A protist causes recurrent fever and can be fatal. The mosquito is the vector, not the pathogen. Life cycle includes mosquitoes. Nets prevent bites; controlling breeding reduces vectors. Plant virus/fungus examples: TMV and rose black spot; see plant-health map.
